claim: Two ferrets were trained on a Go/No-Go delayed categorization task under appetitive reinforcement.
source: Two ferrets were trained on a Go/No-Go delayed categorization task under appetitive reinforcement.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: Water-deprived ferrets had to classify click trains into two categories: target (Go) and non-target (No-Go) depending on the rates of click trains.
source: Water-deprived ferrets had to classify click trains into two categories: target (Go) and non-target (No-Go) depending on the rates of click trains.
evidence: This describes the task structure used in the experiment.

claim: Six rates were used, from 4 to 24 Hz in 4 Hz steps, and with a category boundary fixed at 14 Hz.
source: Six rates were used, from 4 to 24 Hz in 4 Hz steps, and with a category boundary fixed at 14 Hz.
evidence: This specifies the stimulus parameters used in the experiment.

claim: One animal was trained with low rates as the Go sounds, while the second animal classified high rates as the Go sounds.
source: To ensure the dissociation between categories and stimulus rates, one animal was trained with low rates as the Go sounds, while the second animal classified high rates as the Go sounds.
evidence: This describes the counterbalancing of stimulus-category mapping across animals.

claim: Click trains were presented for 1.1 s and were followed by a 1-s-long delay in which the animals had to refrain from licking.
source: Click trains were presented for 1.1 s and were followed by a 1-s-long delay in which the animals had to refrain from licking (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the temporal structure of the task as shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Licks during the subsequent 1-s-long response window were rewarded with water in Go trials and punished with a timeout in No-Go trials.
source: Licks during the subsequent 1-s-long response window were rewarded with water in Go trials and punished with a timeout in No-Go trials.
evidence: This describes the reinforcement contingencies of the task.

claim: Any licks before the response window (early licks) resulted in an aborted trial and were punished with a timeout.
source: Any licks before this response window (early licks) resulted in an aborted trial and were punished with a timeout; these were called 'early trials'.
evidence: This describes the consequences of premature responses.

claim: Ferret P categorized the click trains with d' = 1.2 ± 0.5 (n = 35 sessions).
source: Ferrets categorized the click trains (ferret P: d' = 1.2 ± 0.5, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: d' = 1.1 ± 0.2, n = 39 sessions; Figure 1b)
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral performance data for ferret P.

claim: Ferret T categorized the click trains with d' = 1.1 ± 0.2 (n = 39 sessions).
source: Ferrets categorized the click trains (ferret P: d' = 1.2 ± 0.5, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: d' = 1.1 ± 0.2, n = 39 sessions; Figure 1b)
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral performance data for ferret T.

claim: Ferrets showed a bias to lick for the No-Go rates close to the category boundary (12 Hz).
source: Ferrets categorized the click trains (ferret P: d' = 1.2 ± 0.5, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: d' = 1.1 ± 0.2, n = 39 sessions; Figure 1b) with a bias to lick for the No-Go rates close to the category boundary (12 Hz for the animal shown in Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes a behavioral bias observed in the animals' responses.

claim: The bias to lick for No-Go rates close to the category boundary was found in both ferrets regardless of the mapping between stimulus rates and category.
source: This was found in both ferrets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b) regardless of the mapping between stimulus rates and category, suggesting that their decision criterion was relatively liberal and impulsive.
evidence: This indicates that the behavioral bias was consistent across animals and stimulus mappings.

claim: The ferrets' decision criterion was relatively liberal and impulsive.
source: This was found in both ferrets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b) regardless of the mapping between stimulus rates and category, suggesting that their decision criterion was relatively liberal and impulsive.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral bias observed in the data.

claim: First lick probability was higher in Go than in No-Go trials throughout the entire trial duration.
source: First lick probability was higher in Go than in No-Go trials throughout the entire trial duration (Figure 1c), confirming the categorical response profile.
evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of licking behavior across trial types.

claim: A build-up of lick probability was observed during the delay, with early responses being quite common in Go trials.
source: We also observed a build-up of lick probability during the delay, with early responses being quite common in Go trials.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of licking behavior during the delay period.

claim: A total of 816 units were recorded in A1 (ferret P: 575; ferret T: 241).
source: We chronically recorded neural activity from a total of 816 units in A1 (ferret P: 575; ferret T: 241), while the two animals alternately listened passively to the stimuli or actively engaged in categorizing them.
evidence: This provides the sample size of neural recordings.

claim: Average click responses across all cells showed a significant increase in firing rate relative to baseline activity in all conditions.
source: Figure 1d depicts the average click responses across all cells, showing a significant increase in firing rate relative to baseline activity in all conditions.
evidence: This describes the general neural response pattern to stimuli.

claim: Firing rates steadily ramped up during the delay period in Go trials compared to No-Go's.
source: Firing rates also steadily ramped up during the delay period in Go trials compared to No-Go's (Figure 1d and e; both animals in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This describes the differential neural activity during the delay period for Go vs No-Go trials.

claim: Neurons with significant changes in firing rate during the delay period did not show any modulation of activity during the passive state.
source: Neurons with significant changes in firing rate during the delay period did not show any modulation of activity during the passive state (Figure 1e).
evidence: This indicates that delay period activity is specific to task engagement.

claim: Ranking neurons by delay activity during the passive condition did not reveal a similar pattern in passive or active states.
source: Ranking neurons by delay activity during the passive condition did not reveal a similar pattern neither in passive or active states (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), reflecting a pattern of response specific to the task-engaged delay period.
evidence: This confirms that the delay activity pattern is specific to task engagement.

claim: The firing rates of neurons increased during the delay in the active state (paired t-test active p=0.01, n = 816 units).
source: Additionally, we found that the firing rates of these neurons increased during the delay (Figure 1f, paired t-test active p=0.01, passive p=0.15, n = 816 units; both animals in Figure 1—figure supplement 2; ferret P: active p=0.04, passive p=0.83, n = 575 units; ferret T: active p<0.001, passive p=0.35, n = 241 units).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for increased delay period firing rates during task engagement.

claim: The firing rates of neurons did not significantly increase during the delay in the passive state (paired t-test passive p=0.15, n = 816 units).
source: Additionally, we found that the firing rates of these neurons increased during the delay (Figure 1f, paired t-test active p=0.01, passive p=0.15, n = 816 units; both animals in Figure 1—figure supplement 2; ferret P: active p=0.04, passive p=0.83, n = 575 units; ferret T: active p<0.001, passive p=0.35, n = 241 units).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that delay period activity is specific to task engagement.

claim: Some heterogeneity was observed in the delay activity, with a proportion of neurons showing large suppression during this period.
source: Nevertheless, we noticed some heterogeneity in the delay activity, with a proportion of neurons showing large suppression during this period (top neurons in Figure 1e).
evidence: This describes the diversity of neural responses during the delay period.

claim: During task engagement, population responses steadily discriminated between Go and No-Go categories along the entire course of the trial.
source: During task engagement, population responses steadily discriminated between Go and No-Go categories along the entire course of the trial (Figure 2a, both animals in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the temporal profile of categorical decoding during task engagement.

claim: Decoding accuracy diminished at stimulus offset, but subsequently increased during the delay period, ultimately peaking in the behavioral response window.
source: Decoding accuracy diminished at stimulus offset, but subsequently increased during the delay period, ultimately peaking in the behavioral response window (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of categorical decoding accuracy.

claim: Decoding accuracy in the passive context decreased throughout the delay period.
source: By contrast, accuracy in the passive context decreased throughout the delay period.
evidence: This describes the difference in decoding accuracy between active and passive states during the delay.

claim: The accuracy of passive context decoder was similar to what is observed in the naive animal.
source: The accuracy of passive context decoder was also similar to what is observed in the naive animal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This indicates that passive listening in trained animals resembles naive responses.

claim: Decoding was performed at the single-session level (11.3 ± 4.9 neurons per session for ferret P; n = 35 sessions and 5.2 ± 3.2 neurons per session for ferret T; n = 39 sessions).
source: Note that decoding was performed at the single-session level (11.3 ± 4.9 neurons per session for ferret P; ± SD; n = 35 sessions and 5.2 ± 3.2 neurons per session for ferret T; n = 39 sessions), explaining the modest but above chance-level performance of the decoder.
evidence: This provides methodological details about the decoding analysis.

claim: For both passive and task-engaged sessions, the direction of the decoding axis was mainly preserved during the stimulus epoch.
source: We found that for both passive and task-engaged sessions, the direction of the decoding axis was mainly preserved during the stimulus epoch (black outline in Figure 2b), and the corresponding decoders trained on passive and task-engaged data were correlated (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This indicates stability of the categorical representation during stimulus presentation.

claim: Decoders trained during the stimulus epoch were uncorrelated with the decoding axis during the delay period of the task-engaged condition.
source: Furthermore, these decoders were uncorrelated with the decoding axis during the delay period of the task-engaged condition (white outline in Figure 2b), indicating a behavior-dependent change of the population code at the sound offset.
evidence: This indicates a change in the neural representation at stimulus offset during task engagement.

claim: The delay activity pattern persisted during the response window, as shown by the correlation between delay and response window decoding axes.
source: This delay activity pattern further persisted during the response window, as shown by the correlation between delay and response window decoding axes (pink outline in Figure 2b).
evidence: This indicates continuity of the categorical representation from delay to response window.

claim: The categorical representation in A1 population activity was time-independent throughout the delay and response window epochs.
source: This suggests a time-independent categorical representation in A1 population activity throughout the delay and response window epochs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between delay and response window decoding axes.

claim: During task engagement, the CPD of the category regressor increased during the stimulus period and persisted throughout the delay period, before increasing at the response window.
source: During task engagement, we found that the CPD of the category regressor increased during the stimulus period and persisted throughout the delay period, before increasing at the response window (Figure 2f and h; paired t-test on category regressor, delay vs response window; ferret P: n = 395 neurons, p<0.001; ferret T: n = 203 neurons, p<0.01).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of categorical encoding using regression analysis.

claim: Both task-engaged and passive category CPD were larger than chance during stimulus presentations.
source: Interestingly, both task-engaged and passive category CPD were larger than chance during stimulus presentations (Figure 2f–i), an effect absent in the naive animal (Figure 2i), which indicates training-dependent encoding of categories.
evidence: This indicates that categorical encoding during stimulus presentation is present in both active and passive states but requires training.

claim: The categorical encoding during stimulus presentation was absent in the naive animal.
source: Interestingly, both task-engaged and passive category CPD were larger than chance during stimulus presentations (Figure 2f–i), an effect absent in the naive animal (Figure 2i), which indicates training-dependent encoding of categories.
evidence: This indicates that categorical encoding requires training.

claim: Categorical encoding during stimulus presentation indicates training-dependent encoding of categories.
source: Interestingly, both task-engaged and passive category CPD were larger than chance during stimulus presentations (Figure 2f–i), an effect absent in the naive animal (Figure 2i), which indicates training-dependent encoding of categories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference between trained and naive animals.

claim: Similar category axes were found in the passive and active conditions when accounting for licks and rewards.
source: We found similar category axes in the passive and active conditions when accounting for licks and rewards (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This indicates that the categorical representation is not confounded by motor or reward-related activity.

claim: Categorical responses revealed a stable encoding of categories during sound presentation, regardless of the stimulus identity.
source: Projections on the category neural axis (called thereafter categorical responses) revealed a stable encoding of categories during sound presentation, regardless of the stimulus identity (Figure 3a and b), indicating that these categorical responses were not contaminated by sensory activity.
evidence: This indicates that categorical encoding is independent of specific stimulus features.

claim: Categories were effectively present in both passive and task-engaged states during stimulus presentation with equal magnitude.
source: We found that categories were effectively present in both passive and task-engaged states during stimulus presentation with equal magnitude (Figure 3a and b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This indicates that categorical encoding during stimulus presentation is not dependent on task engagement.

claim: Significant categories were found only in the task-engaged state during the delay period.
source: In contrast, significant categories were found only in the task-engaged state during the delay period (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This indicates that categorical encoding during the delay period requires task engagement.

claim: No-Go categorical responses aligned with the pre-stimulus spontaneous activity during task engagement.
source: Here, we found that there was a clear shift of population coding between the two behavioral conditions: No-Go categorical responses aligned with the pre-stimulus spontaneous activity during task engagement (Figure 3a), inducing an asymmetry between No-Go and Go categorical responses (Figure 3e, both animals in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and d), a characteristic that is not observed in the passive projections (Figure 3b).
evidence: This describes a task-dependent suppression of No-Go responses.

claim: Task engagement induced an asymmetry between No-Go and Go categorical responses.
source: Here, we found that there was a clear shift of population coding between the two behavioral conditions: No-Go categorical responses aligned with the pre-stimulus spontaneous activity during task engagement (Figure 3a), inducing an asymmetry between No-Go and Go categorical responses (Figure 3e, both animals in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and d), a characteristic that is not observed in the passive projections (Figure 3b).
evidence: This describes a task-dependent change in categorical representation.

claim: The No-Go suppression was confined to the stimulus period (ferret P: p<10–6, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–4, n = 39 sessions).
source: A No-Go suppression index measuring the relative displacement of the No-Go responses closer to the projections of spontaneous activity (Figure 3f) showed that the suppression was confined to the stimulus period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e and f, bottom row; ferret P: p<10–6, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–4, n = 39 sessions), and absent in the delay period (ferret P: p=0.70; ferret T: p=0.46).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the temporal specificity of No-Go suppression.

claim: The No-Go suppression was absent in the delay period (ferret P: p=0.70; ferret T: p=0.46).
source: A No-Go suppression index measuring the relative displacement of the No-Go responses closer to the projections of spontaneous activity (Figure 3f) showed that the suppression was confined to the stimulus period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e and f, bottom row; ferret P: p<10–6, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–4, n = 39 sessions), and absent in the delay period (ferret P: p=0.70; ferret T: p=0.46).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that No-Go suppression is specific to the stimulus period.

claim: Projections of the passive population responses onto the active category neural axis did not show the suppression of No-Go sounds.
source: Crucially, projections of the passive population responses onto the active category neural axis did not show the suppression of No-Go sounds, confirming that this shift originated from a change in the structure of the population responses during task engagement, and not due to the weights of the regressor themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This confirms that the No-Go suppression is due to changes in neural activity, not analysis artifacts.

claim: The categorical signal in the stimulus period exhibits short latencies consistent with a feedforward mechanism of early categorization taking place in A1.
source: The categorical signal in the stimulus period exhibits short latencies (Figure 3a) consistent with a feedforward mechanism of early categorization taking place in A1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing of categorical responses.

claim: The categorical axes in the early stimulus and delay periods were not correlated.
source: However, the categorical axes in the early stimulus and delay periods were not correlated (white frames in Figure 4a).
evidence: This indicates that the neural representation changes between stimulus and delay periods.

claim: The single-trial fluctuations of categorical responses in the stimulus and delay periods were correlated (p<0.001, permutation test, n = 74 sessions).
source: Specifically, we examined the single-trial fluctuations of categorical responses in each period and discovered that the two categorical responses were correlated (one session in Figure 4b, all sessions in the inset; p<0.001, permutation test, n = 74 sessions).
evidence: This indicates a link between categorical information during stimulus and delay periods despite different neural axes.

claim: The stimulus and delay categorical responses were computed from uncorrelated projection axes that were originally derived from distinct non-overlapping epochs.
source: Note that the stimulus and delay categorical responses were computed from uncorrelated projection axes (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) that were originally derived from distinct non-overlapping epochs, and hence the single-trial fluctuations in categorical responses need not have been correlated in any way.
evidence: This emphasizes the significance of the correlation between stimulus and delay categorical responses.

claim: Categorical activity built up during the delay period and culminated when the animal licked.
source: By aligning single-trial projections onto lick timings during the response window, we found that the categorical activity built up during the delay period and culminated when the animal licked (Figure 4d, categorical responses centered on licks), indicating that delay activity was anticipating behavioral responses.
evidence: This indicates that delay activity is related to motor preparation or decision commitment.

claim: Significantly faster response build-up rates were found in early trials than in hit trials.
source: We found significantly faster response build-up rates in early trials than in hit trials (Figure 4c).
evidence: This indicates that the rate of categorical response build-up correlates with reaction time.

claim: Early trials with early licks in the delay exhibited the steepest response build-ups.
source: Early trials with early licks in the delay exhibited the steepest response build-ups (Figure 4c), a pattern that was not observed in the categorical responses during the stimulus period (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This indicates that the build-up rate is specific to the delay period and correlates with reaction time.

claim: Categorical responses of early and hit trials culminated at the licking time when aligned to reaction times.
source: We then aligned all trials to their respective reaction times and found that categorical responses of early and hit trials culminated at the licking time (Figure 4d).
evidence: This indicates that categorical responses are tightly linked to behavioral output.

claim: Decoding accuracy during delay for incorrect trials was at chance level (p=0.99, permutation test).
source: That was not the case, but instead we found a decrease in decoding accuracy during the sound period and a decoding performance at chance level during the delay (Figure 5a and b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for separate projections of false alarm and miss trials; decoding accuracy during delay for incorrect trials: p=0.99, permutation test).
evidence: This indicates that categorical information is degraded during error trials.

claim: Decoding accuracy dipped below chance during the response window, confirming that motor information was confined to this late time period.
source: As a control, we noted that decoding accuracy dipped below chance during the response window confirming that motor information was confined to this late time period (Figure 5a).
evidence: This indicates that the decoder captures motor-related activity during the response window.

claim: Incorrect decisions could be traced back to the stimulus period.
source: This indicates that incorrect decisions could be traced back to the stimulus period, excluding hypothesis (b) in which only the delay activity was incorrect during error trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding results for error trials.

claim: Sensory responses were lower in incorrect compared to correct trials during the stimulus period (ferret P: p<10–5, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–3, n = 39 sessions).
source: In line with this interpretation, we found that sensory responses were lower in incorrect compared to correct trials (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a and b; stimulus period-sensory index: ferret P: p<10–5, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–3, n = 39 sessions; stimulus period-category index: ferret P: p=0.01, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p=0.35, n = 39 sessions; paired t-test across sessions, individual boxes were tested with permutation test).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that sensory encoding is degraded during error trials.

claim: Categorical responses were degraded during the delay period in error trials (ferret P: p<10–4, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–5, n = 39 sessions).
source: Categorical responses were further degraded during the delay period (delay-category index [Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c] for both animals; paired t-test across sessions; ferret P: p<10–4, n = 35 sessions; ferret T: p<10–5, n = 39 sessions).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that categorical encoding is degraded during the delay in error trials.

claim: Errors likely originated from an improper encoding of the stimulus that subsequently led to an incorrect categorization and behavioral response.
source: Altogether, this suggests that errors likely originated from an improper encoding of the stimulus that subsequently led to an incorrect categorization and behavioral response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the degraded sensory and categorical encoding during error trials.

claim: Categorical perception of real-world signals is thought to be implemented at higher cortical levels.
source: Categorical perception of real-world signals is a key cognitive function in all sensory modalities, one that is thought to be implemented at higher cortical levels (Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012; Folstein et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2020; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Roy et al., 2010; Bizley and Cohen, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: An encoding of behavioral categories was isolated in the population-average during stimulus presentation in both task-engaged and passive listening.
source: First, we isolated an encoding of behavioral categories in the population-average during stimulus presentation in both task-engaged and passive listening.
evidence: This is a summary of one of the main findings of the study.

claim: Categorical encoding during stimulus presentation was not observed in a naive animal.
source: This was not observed in a naive animal (Figure 2i).
evidence: This indicates that categorical encoding requires training.

claim: The categorical encoding during stimulus presentation is interpreted as an effect of long-term memory.
source: We interpret this observation as an effect of long-term memory (Elgueda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the training-dependent categorical encoding, supported by a citation.

claim: Population-level categorical responses to No-Go sounds were suppressed during task engagement during the stimulus period.
source: Second, we found that population-level categorical responses to No-Go sounds were suppressed during task engagement during the stimulus period (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of one of the main findings of the study.

claim: The population-level categorical representation changed at stimulus offset but still correlated at the single-trial level with categorical responses observed during the stimulus period.
source: Third, the population-level categorical representation changed at stimulus offset but still correlated at the single-trial level with categorical responses observed during the stimulus period (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a summary of one of the main findings of the study.

claim: Incorrect behavioral choices were traced back to degraded categorical encoding during the stimulus period, resulting in a degraded categorical representation during the subsequent delay period.
source: Fourth, incorrect behavioral choices were traced back to degraded categorical encoding during the stimulus period, resulting in a degraded categorical representation during the subsequent delay period (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of one of the main findings of the study.

claim: Behavior-dependent categorical information emerged during the stimulus period, influenced population dynamics beyond the stimulus period itself, and persisted throughout the delay period until the behavioral response.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that behavior-dependent categorical information emerged during the stimulus period, influenced population dynamics beyond the stimulus period itself, and persisted throughout the delay period until the behavioral response.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the main findings of the study.

claim: Previous findings have found categorical responses in A1 with a marked increase of response contrast at category boundaries.
source: Previous findings have found categorical responses in A1 with a marked increase of response contrast at category boundaries (Yin et al., 2020; Xin et al., 2019)⁠.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The encoding of stimulus sensory properties within behavioral categories was stable across behavioral states.
source: Similar to a previous study in the mouse (Xin et al., 2019⁠), we found that the encoding of stimulus sensory properties within behavioral categories was stable across behavioral states.
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous research.

claim: Xin et al., 2019 found that categorical representations in A1 matched behavioral decision as early as at stimulus offset, and was maintained during several seconds.
source: In Xin et al., 2019⁠, the authors found that categorical representations in A1 matched behavioral decision as early as at stimulus offset, and was maintained during several seconds.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings.

claim: Choice-related activity has been demonstrated to be the result of feedforward and feedback flow between primary sensory cortices and downstream regions.
source: Such choice-related activity has been demonstrated to be the result of feedforward and feedback flow between primary sensory cortices and downstream regions (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Yang et al., 2016⁠).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanisms underlying choice-related activity, supported by citations.

claim: The current observations are consistent with the view that choice-related activity results from feedforward and feedback flow between primary sensory cortices and downstream regions.
source: Our observations are consistent with this view as we found that perceptual choice influenced the category decoded during the response window (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of previous research.

claim: The use of longer stimulus followed by a long delay allowed decoupling of early categorical information building up during stimulus presentation from the late choice report of the animal.
source: Nevertheless, we used longer stimulus followed by a long delay in our study, which allowed us to decouple the early categorical information building up during stimulus presentation from the late choice report of the animal.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage of the current study.

claim: Categorical information declined during stimulus and delay periods in error trials, suggesting that incorrect trials were due to a lack of proper categorical information early on during the stimulus itself.
source: In addition, categorical information declined during stimulus and delay periods, suggesting that incorrect trials were due to a lack of proper categorical information early on during the stimulus itself.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the error trial analysis.

claim: The asymmetry in the categorical representation stems from a task-induced population-level enhancement of Go and suppression of No-Go categorical responses.
source: Instead, this asymmetry in the categorical representation stems from a task-induced population-level enhancement of Go and suppression of No-Go categorical responses, consistent with our previous findings (Bagur et al., 2018) in these Go/No-Go paradigms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the No-Go suppression finding, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: No-Go sounds instruct the animal to maintain the same behavioral output (lick inhibition) as in periods of silence when spontaneous activity is measured.
source: To elaborate, No-Go sounds instruct the animal to maintain the same behavioral output (lick inhibition) as in periods of silence when spontaneous activity is measured.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral meaning of No-Go sounds.

claim: The alignment of the No-Go population responses with the spontaneous activity reflects the identical behavioral meaning of these two epochs.
source: We therefore proposed that the alignment of the No-Go population responses with the spontaneous activity reflects the identical behavioral meaning of these two epochs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the No-Go suppression finding.

claim: Population dynamics could multiplex behavior-independent sensory representations and task-modulated categorical encoding.
source: This suggests an interesting mechanism in which population dynamics could multiplex behavior-independent sensory representations and task-modulated categorical encoding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: The multiplexing of sensory and categorical information is reminiscent of population dynamics found in prefrontal cortex.
source: Intriguingly, this is reminiscent of population dynamics found in prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Mante et al., 2013), where sensory information and decision formation were represented along different neural dimensions.
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous research in PFC.

claim: Categorical information was degraded in error trials, which is consistent with an early mapping of individual stimulus into generic categories at the level of primary sensory areas.
source: In line with a role of A1 in the category build-up, we found that categorical information was degraded in error trials, which is consistent with an early mapping of individual stimulus into generic categories at the level of primary sensory areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the error trial findings.

claim: A1 has an initial contribution in the feedforward formation of behavior-dependent categories.
source: We thus propose that A1 has an initial contribution in the feedfoward formation of behavior-dependent categories.
evidence: This is a proposed role for A1 based on the findings.

claim: During behavior, higher areas would access an explicit representation of the behaviorally relevant categories by reading out the asymmetrical population-level encoding of Go and No-Go sounds in A1.
source: During behavior, higher areas would access an explicit representation of the behaviorally relevant categories by reading out the asymmetrical population-level encoding of Go and No-Go sounds in A1 (Bagur et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for how higher areas use A1 categorical information.

claim: Higher areas would utilize the A1 categorical representation to amplify and strengthen the ongoing category, possibly passing or gating it to motor-related regions depending on the behavioral state.
source: These areas would then utilize the A1 categorical representation to amplify and strengthen the ongoing category, possibly passing or gating it to motor-related regions depending on the behavioral state (Atiani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for how categorical information is used downstream of A1.

claim: Categorical responses changed at stimulus offset to maintain a Go-specific prolonged activity during the delay period.
source: Categorical responses changed at stimulus offset to maintain a Go-specific prolonged activity during the delay period, consistent with other studies showing choice-related activity in A1 (Bizley et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2012b; Niwa et al., 2012a; Guo et al., 2019⁠).
evidence: This is a summary of the delay period findings, supported by citations to related work.

claim: The delay activity is not interpreted as efferent copies directly sent from motor regions.
source: We do not interpret this activity as efferent copies directly sent from motor regions (Schneider et al., 2018), as one would expect such motor-related activity to have shorter latencies (~100–300 ms; Bagur et al., 2018; Orlandi et al., 2023⁠).
evidence: This is an interpretation ruling out one possible explanation for delay activity.

claim: Sound category was decodable throughout the entire delay period, which does not match with short-latency efference copies.
source: Here, sound category was decodable throughout the entire delay period (Figure 2a), which does not match with short-latency efference copies.
evidence: This provides evidence against the efference copy interpretation.

claim: The delay activity is not closely locked in time to licks since false alarm trials were not decoded as hit trials during the delay period.
source: We have also found that the delay activity is not closely locked in time to licks since false alarm trials, in which the animals licked during the response window, were not decoded as hit trials during the delay period (Figure 5b).
evidence: This provides evidence that delay activity is not simply motor-related.

claim: Other studies investigating the role of A1 in auditory Go/No-Go tasks with a delay did not analyze neuronal responses after Go sounds.
source: Other studies investigating the role of A1 in auditory Go/No-Go tasks with a delay did not analyze neuronal responses after Go sounds (Yu et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2016), which may explain why this sustained activity has not been previously reported.
evidence: This explains why the delay activity finding is novel.

claim: Delay activity in sensory cortices is thought not to be causally involved in the behavioral response of trained animals.
source: Interestingly, delay activity in sensory cortices is thought not to be causally involved in the behavioral response of trained animals (causal inactivations in V1 [Goard et al., 2016⁠] and A1 [Yu et al., 2021⁠]).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research on the causal role of delay activity.

claim: Delay activity in A1 could be the result of a feedback signal from higher-order decision-related areas signaling the chosen category and maintaining it in memory.
source: First, delay activity in A1 could be the result of a feedback signal from higher-order decision-related areas signaling the chosen category and maintaining it in memory by engaging A1 in a network of parietal and frontal areas (Goard et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: This is one possible interpretation of the delay activity.

claim: Previous works in the somatosensory system have shown that choice-related information flows bidirectionally between primary and secondary somatosensory cortices.
source: In this framework, previous works in the somatosensory system have shown that choice-related information flows bidirectionally between primary and secondary somatosensory cortices, with choice-related information emerging in primary sensory cortex, then fed to downstream areas that further feedback enriched choice-related information to the primary field (Kwon et al., 2016⁠).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research supporting the feedback interpretation.

claim: Trial-to-trial fluctuations of categorical responses during the sound period correlate with the amplitude of the delay categorical signal, possibly suggesting that category-related information during the stimulus and delay periods is part of a communication loop.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we have demonstrated that trial-to-trial fluctuations of categorical responses during the sound period correlate with the amplitude of the delay categorical signal (Figure 4b), possibly suggesting that category-related information during the stimulus and delay periods is part of this communication loop.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between stimulus and delay categorical responses.

claim: Delay activity could be the result of motor preparation that would unfold over several hundreds of milliseconds.
source: A second interpretation is that delay activity is the result of motor preparation that would unfold over several hundreds of milliseconds (Musall et al., 2019⁠).
evidence: This is another possible interpretation of the delay activity.

claim: The pattern of activity observed during early trials is consistent with the motor preparation interpretation, with faster build-up when the animals licked earlier.
source: The pattern of activity observed during early trials is consistent with this view, with faster build-up when the animals licked earlier.
evidence: This provides evidence supporting the motor preparation interpretation.

claim: A similar pattern of faster build-up in early trials was not observed on false alarm trials, contrary to what would be predicted for the motor preparation interpretation.
source: However, a similar pattern was not observed on false alarm trials, contrary to what would be predicted for this interpretation.
evidence: This provides evidence against the motor preparation interpretation.

claim: Delay activity could signal reward expectation.
source: A last possibility is that delay activity signals reward expectation (Chubykin et al., 2013⁠), a type of response which increases through learning (Musall et al., 2019; Poort et al., 2015⁠).
evidence: This is another possible interpretation of the delay activity.

claim: Delay activity could reflect post-learning residual top-down feedback, or alternatively may be the signature of an eligibility trace necessary for bridging the gap between the sound and the response window.
source: This delay activity would then reflect post-learning residual top-down feedback, or alternatively may be the signature of an eligibility trace, that is, a persistent activity necessary for bridging the gap between the sound and the response window (Raybuck and Lattal, 2014⁠).
evidence: This provides two possible mechanisms for reward expectation-related delay activity.

claim: Disentangling the different interpretations of delay activity will require further experiments.
source: Overall, disentangling these different interpretations will require further experiments.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the current study in determining the exact nature of delay activity.

claim: Adult female ferrets (Mustela putorius furo) obtained from Marshall BioResource were used for this study.
source: Adult female ferrets (Mustela putorius furo) obtained from Marshall BioResource were used for this study.
evidence: This describes the animal subjects used in the study.

claim: The animals were 1–3 years of age, weighing 500–800 g.
source: The animals were 1–3 years of age, weighing 500–800 g, and were housed in pairs or trios with a normal day–night light cycle and free access to water during weekends.
evidence: This provides details about the animal subjects.

claim: Ferrets were on a water-controlled protocol in which their water intake is restricted during the weekdays.
source: Ferrets were on a water-controlled protocol in which their water intake is restricted during the weekdays.
evidence: This describes the water restriction protocol used for behavioral training.

claim: Water was delivered during behavioral sessions as a reward.
source: Water was delivered during behavioral sessions as a reward.
evidence: This describes the reinforcement used in the behavioral task.

claim: The animals' weights were daily monitored and maintained at 80% of pre-experiment weight.
source: The animals' weights were daily monitored and maintained at 80% of pre-experiment weight.
evidence: This describes the animal care protocol.
